kernels.l1: Two jobs: push the first one, and check each one touches the next.
kernels.l2: To be sure a rule keeps working, do two jobs. Show it works the very first time. Then show that whenever it works once, it works the next time too.
kernels.l3: An induction proof has three parts: say exactly what the claim is and where it starts, check the first case, and show that any case being true forces the next one to be true. Assuming one case is not cheating, because you are only proving an if–then.
kernels.l4: State the claim and where it starts; prove the first case; then prove that each case forces the next, for an arbitrary case. The step is a conditional, so assuming one case in order to reach the next is a hypothesis, not circular reasoning.
kernels.l5: The step is a claim about every case at once — *if this one holds, the next does* — which is why you are allowed to assume the case you are working from. The first case anchors the chain.
kernels.l6: Induction is valid because the counting numbers have no infinite descent: a least counterexample would contradict either the base case or the step.
kernels.l7: An induction proof states the claim and where it starts, proves the first case, and shows that any one case forces the next. That last part is a conditional, which is why assuming the case you are working from is not circular.
kernels.l8: Base case, inductive hypothesis, inductive step — and the step must run from the assumed case toward the next one, not backwards from what is to be shown. Assuming the conclusion and reaching something true proves nothing.

kernel: (1) State A(n) and the starting value n₀. (2) Prove the base case A(n₀). (3) Prove the inductive step: assume A(k) for some k ≥ n₀, deduce A(k+1). The inductive step is a conditional, so assuming A(k) is not circular.
objectives: Write the three steps for a given claim
Explain why the step is not begging the question
